17 AI System Concepts Every Founder Should Understand Before Hiring an AI Agency

A founder once sent me an agency proposal that used 16 of these 17 terms. It did not contain a single number. The 1 term it skipped was evaluations.

Founders read charts like this as a shopping list. I read them as a bill of materials. Every box is something you pay for, maintain, and get blamed for when it breaks in front of a customer. Here is how I break it down.

4 of these boxes decide whether you have a product. Embeddings, vector databases, RAG, and context engineering. This is the part everyone demos. Getting it 80% right takes a week. The last 15% takes months, and that 15% is where your customer decides whether to trust it.

3 of them decide whether you have a business. Semantic caching, model routing, and an AI gateway. None of them show up in a demo, and together they set your gross margin. I once audited a product that lost money on every paying user because every question, including "what are your opening hours," went to the largest model available. Routing and caching fixed it in 2 weeks and cut inference spend by more than half.

5 of them decide how much risk you carry. Function calling, tool use, MCP, external integrations, and the agent harness. This is where AI starts writing to your CRM, sending emails, touching money. Every capability you hand an agent is a liability until you can prove how it behaves. My month 1 default: the agent drafts, a person approves.

3 of them decide whether it still works in month 6. The execution loop, memory, and guardrails. Most agent failures I get called in to fix live here. A loop that never terminates. Memory that leaks 1 customer's context into another's session. Guardrails added after a bad answer reached a client.

And 2 of them decide whether the other 15 are real. Observability and evaluations. If an agency cannot show you a test set, a baseline score, and a trace of every request in the first 2 weeks, you have no way to know what you are paying for.

So the most useful question to ask any agency is which of the 17 they would leave out, and why. Most products I scope need 8 to 10. Some need a classifier and a well-written SQL query, and I tell founders that on the first call, even when it shrinks my contract.

That is also why clients stay with me for years. From week 1, they own the evaluation set, the dashboards, and the cost per query. After that, every decision is based on numbers they can see, so the work shifts from building the system to growing it.

I am Muhammad Ghulam Jillani, Founder and CEO at Jillani SofTech. 22+ production AI systems across Healthcare, Finance, Legal, and SaaS.

Planning an AI product, or holding an agency proposal you doubt? Book 30 minutes with me today, free. Bring the plan or the proposal. You leave knowing which of the 17 you need, which ones are missing, and what the build should cost.

17 AI System Concepts Every Founder Should Understand Before Hiring an AI Agency

A founder once sent me an agency proposal that used 16 of these 17 terms. It did not contain a single number. The 1 term it skipped was evaluations.

Founders read charts like this as a shopping list. I read them as a bill of materials. Every box is something you pay for, maintain, and get blamed for when it breaks in front of a customer. Here is how I break it down.

4 of these boxes decide whether you have a product. Embeddings, vector databases, RAG, and context engineering. This is the part everyone demos. Getting it 80% right takes a week. The last 15% takes months, and that 15% is where your customer decides whether to trust it.

3 of them decide whether you have a business. Semantic caching, model routing, and an AI gateway. None of them show up in a demo, and together they set your gross margin. I once audited a product that lost money on every paying user because every question, including "what are your opening hours," went to the largest model available. Routing and caching fixed it in 2 weeks and cut inference spend by more than half.

5 of them decide how much risk you carry. Function calling, tool use, MCP, external integrations, and the agent harness. This is where AI starts writing to your CRM, sending emails, touching money. Every capability you hand an agent is a liability until you can prove how it behaves. My month 1 default: the agent drafts, a person approves.

3 of them decide whether it still works in month 6. The execution loop, memory, and guardrails. Most agent failures I get called in to fix live here. A loop that never terminates. Memory that leaks 1 customer's context into another's session. Guardrails added after a bad answer reached a client.

And 2 of them decide whether the other 15 are real. Observability and evaluations. If an agency cannot show you a test set, a baseline score, and a trace of every request in the first 2 weeks, you have no way to know what you are paying for.

So the most useful question to ask any agency is which of the 17 they would leave out, and why. Most products I scope need 8 to 10. Some need a classifier and a well-written SQL query, and I tell founders that on the first call, even when it shrinks my contract.

That is also why clients stay with me for years. From week 1, they own the evaluation set, the dashboards, and the cost per query. After that, every decision is based on numbers they can see, so the work shifts from building the system to growing it.

I am Muhammad Ghulam Jillani, Founder and CEO at Jillani SofTech. 22+ production AI systems across Healthcare, Finance, Legal, and SaaS.

Planning an AI product, or holding an agency proposal you doubt? Book 30 minutes with me today, free. Bring the plan or the proposal. You leave knowing which of the 17 you need, which ones are missing, and what the build should cost.

Earlier this year, I got absolutely hammered in the comments for saying AI was already rejecting candidates.

I was told I was spreading misinformation.

That AI “doesn’t reject anyone”.

That a human always makes the final decision.

That I clearly didn’t understand how recruitment technology worked. Despite two decades in Talent, including running a global Talent Acquisition function, I found that last one particularly entertaining.

Well, Mobley v. Workday is becoming a case every Talent, People and HR Tech leader should be paying attention to.

Its alleged that Workday’s applicant-screening tools discriminate on the basis of age, race and disability. Workday denies wrongdoing of course, and, the court has not found that Workday discriminated against applicants… yet. The case is ongoing. 

But something significant has already happened.

A US federal court found that the allegations were sufficient for Workday potentially to be treated as an agent of its employer customers, because employers were alleged to have delegated parts of the traditional hiring function, including advancing or rejecting candidates to its technology. 

And the age-discrimination element has already been allowed to proceed as a nationwide collective action covering applicants aged 40+ who applied through Workday from September 2020 onwards. 

That should make ALL employers sit up.

Not because it proves every automated rejection is discriminatory. It doesn’t and I’m not saying that. 

But if the litigation establishes discriminatory impact, I would expect some very uncomfortable questions to follow about what employers knew, what they configured, what they monitored and what evidence they retained.

So, if AI or any algorithmic tools touch your recruitment process, I’d be asking now:

1) Where does automation actually sit in our funnel? Sourcing? Ranking? Screening? Rejection? Interview selection?

2) Which decisions can happen without human intervention?

3) Have we tested outcomes? Not whether the vendor says the product is compliant, what does our own candidate data show?

4) Can we analyse progression and rejection rates across protected groups where legally permitted?

5) What have we configured ourselves? Knockout questions, scoring rules, experience requirements and other criteria matter.

6) What does the contract say about audit rights, liability and access to decision data?

7) Could we explain why Candidate A progressed and Candidate B didn’t?

8) What evidence are we keeping? Because “the system did it” is going to be a very poor governance strategy.

There is a bigger point here. Buying AI doesn’t outsource accountability, and, deploying technology you don’t understand into a process that determines who gets access to employment is a governance decision, not simply a procurement decision.

In London 10 days ago we showcased a map.

Four locations of a fictional retail and hospitality group: two stores, two hotels. 48 seasonal hires starting across eight different Mondays. Click a location and you see who starts when, what is signed, what is missing.

Nobody asked about the map. They asked what was underneath it.

Underneath it was a workflow. The hiring process, described in plain language, built into steps that run the same way every time. Right-to-work check, contract, uniform, system access, first-day schedule. AI where a step needs judgment. A manager where a decision needs a person.

The map was just one way of looking at that workflow. It was built in an afternoon with a single prompt on top of our workflow layer, and works with any AI tool.

That is the shift I keep trying to describe.

For twenty years software started with the screen. Someone designed the interface and the process bent to fit it.

Now you start with the process. You describe how hiring, onboarding or offboarding should actually work. You decide which steps must be identical every time and which need a human. Then you work backwards to whatever view you want: a map, a dashboard, a Slack message, a spreadsheet, nothing at all.

The interface is becoming the cheap part. The process, the data and the governance underneath are what last.

Every Bad Hire Has a Price Tag But Most Organizations Never See the Full Bill.

We talked about this already.
A bad hire is expensive but a limited talent search makes it worse. But let be more realistic, most organizations only count the obvious costs, the salary paid, the time lost in recruitment and the onboarding investment written off, but the real bill goes much deeper than that.

A bad hire costs you the productivity of every team member affected by the wrong fit. It costs you, the morale of a team that now has to compensate for someone who should not have been there, the clients who noticed the drop in quality, the projects that stalled, the culture that quietly shifted in the wrong direction, and then there is the cost of starting all over again.

Most studies put the true cost of a bad hire at anywhere between 50% to 200% of that person's annual salary, and that is before you factor in the ripple effect on your employer brand.

So the question is not "Can we afford to hire better?" but rather "Can we afford not to?"

A lot of predictions focus purely on technology — AI screening, automated onboarding, predictive attrition models. Those tools are real and growing. But the function underneath them isn't changing nearly as much as the headlines suggest.

Here's what's genuinely changing 👇

🔄 The tools — AI-assisted sourcing, predictive people analytics, automated administrative work freeing up time for higher-value conversations 🔄 The workforce structure — more contract, freelance, and hybrid arrangements requiring more flexible HR frameworks 🔄 Expectations around transparency — pay ranges, growth paths, and company values are expected to be visible upfront, not discovered later 🔄 The definition of benefits — mental health support, flexible work, and personalized total rewards increasingly matter as much as traditional perks 🔄 Speed of change itself — HR now has to build systems that can adapt quickly, rather than static five-year policy documents

Here's what isn't changing, no matter how advanced the tools get 👇

🔒 People still need to feel heard — no algorithm replaces an honest conversation with a manager who actually listens 🔒 Trust still has to be earned — through consistency and follow-through, not policy language alone 🔒 Fair treatment still matters most — candidates and employees still judge companies by how they're actually treated, not by how sophisticated the tech stack is 🔒 Good management remains the biggest lever — no tool fixes a bad manager; it can only support a good one 🔒 Culture is still built through daily behavior — not stated values, not a careers page, but what leadership actually does when it's inconvenient

The real skill for HR professionals going forward isn't just learning new tools — it's knowing which parts of the job technology can genuinely improve, and which parts will always require real human judgment and care.

Fifty posts into this series, that's really been the throughline: better HR isn't about more process or more tech. It's about consistently choosing to treat people like people, even as everything else around that responsibility keeps evolving.

I've tried both Upwork and LinkedIn for landing Android contracts.
One made me $200/month. One made me $4,000/month.
Here's the honest breakdown of why.

I'm not here to bash Upwork. I'm here to give you honest data.

Upwork - the reality in 2026:
→ Brutal competition on price, you're bidding against $8/hr developers
→ Upwork takes 10-20% of every contract
→ JSS score takes 3-6 months to build from zero
→ Platform controls the relationship, disputes favour clients
→ Clients on Upwork are price-sensitive by nature (they're on a freelance platform)
→ Works well for: quick gigs, building initial portfolio, specific niches

LinkedIn- the reality in 2026:
→ Clients come to you based on perceived authority
→ Zero platform fee on direct contracts
→ Relationship is yours not mediated
→ Clients are budget-qualified (they're not on a price comparison platform)
→ Requires: consistent content, 3-6 month runway before results
→ Works well for: senior engineers, long-term contracts, premium rates

The strategy I used:
Upwork: active first 6 months to build portfolio and case studies.
LinkedIn: long-term channel for inbound. 3-5 posts/week minimum.
The Upwork portfolio funds the LinkedIn runway.

Where most engineers go wrong:
→ Spending years on Upwork competing on price instead of building LinkedIn authority
→ Starting LinkedIn and quitting after 3 weeks because 'it doesn't work'
→ Not treating content as a 6-12 month investment

The $200/month was Upwork in month 1.
The $4,000/month came from LinkedIn in month 6.
The 6 months felt slow. They were actually fast.

Which platform are you using right now for client acquisition? And what's your experience?

Build long-term relationships with pharmacy colleges, biotechnology universities, life sciences institutions and engineering colleges based on workforce requirements, programme strength, research capabilities and placement outcomes.

2. Campus Segmentation
Map institutions to specific talent requirements - Production, QA, QC, R&D, Regulatory Affairs, Clinical Operations, Engineering, Supply Chain and Commercial functions.

3. Employer Branding
Engage students before placement season through guest lectures, technical webinars, plant visits, innovation challenges, research collaborations and industry projects.

4. Internship-to-Hire Pipelines
Use internships to evaluate technical capability, learning potential and workplace readiness while giving students practical exposure to pharmaceutical operations.

5. Structured Campus Assessment
Standardise screening and interviews across large applicant volumes. AI-assisted screening can help match academic backgrounds, projects and skills with predefined role requirements, while structured video interviews support consistent evaluation.

6. Graduate Development
Campus hiring doesn’t end with an offer letter. GMP training, technical learning, mentoring, performance management and defined career paths help convert fresh graduates into capable long-term professionals.

7. Workforce Planning
Align campus hiring with future requirements across manufacturing, quality, R&D, regulatory, engineering and supply chain instead of hiring only against immediate vacancies.

The shift is from campus placements as an annual activity → campus recruitment as a continuous talent pipeline.

Coffee in Raleigh. Technology in Chennai.

… I have a little history with Starbucks.

Over the years, I worked with Starbucks leadership and recruited many of the people who helped build its early digital capabilities.

So today’s news caught my attention.

📌 What Changed

▪ Starbucks → builds Chennai technology hub
▪ SoftServe → Andriy Stytsyuk named CEO
▪ Microsoft → fourth India cloud region goes live
▪ HFS Research + Capgemini → AI pricing gets harder
▪ H-1B → talent model faces more pressure

⸻

☕ GCC Signal

Starbucks m is building its first India technology hub in Chennai, with plans for roughly 800 technology jobs.

But here is the GDCF signal:

CTO Anand Varadarajan says the company intends to bring more work currently performed by third-party service providers in-house over time.

GDCFs are helping enterprises build GCCs while those same enterprises increasingly build technology capability of their own.

That is a boundary worth watching over a cup of coffee. 

⸻

👔 Executive Signal

SoftServe named longtime executive Andriy Stytsyuk CEO, effective October 1.

Stytsyuk spent 16 years inside the company and currently serves as COO and CFO. The board selected him after a year-long process to lead SoftServe’s next phase of growth.

An internal operator taking the top job at a global AI and technology services firm.

Congratulations, Andriy. We will be watching what comes next.

⸻

📈 Infrastructure Signal

Microsoft’s fourth India cloud region is now live in Hyderabad.

Puneet Chandok says India South Central turns part of Microsoft’s $20.5B commitment into operating infrastructure — with India positioned as a strategic AI hub for Asia and the Global South.

India’s advantage is no longer simply labor.

Talent + GCCs + infrastructure + AI capability are converging.

⸻

📉 Commercial Signal

New HFS Research with Capgemini shows financial-services companies are experimenting with outcome pricing while traditional FTE, SLA and license models still anchor most AI contracts.

HFS says providers increasingly need to become “commercial architects.”

That raises a recruiting question I am going to keep researching:

Who are those people — and are GDCFs actually hiring and developing them?

⸻

🧠 The Recruiting Guy Take

Not every Monday needs one giant thesis.

Today I am watching the boundaries.

Clients are building capability. Hyperscalers are building infrastructure. GDCFs are changing leadership. And the commercial model is still trying to catch up.

When the model changes, eventually the talent model has to follow.

⸻

❓ Question of the Day

As enterprises build more technology capability in-house, what should they still buy from GDCF rainmakers?

"Sovereign AI" stopped being a government-only concern in 2026. Regulated industries — healthcare, financial services, defense — are now among the fastest movers toward keeping their AI infrastructure entirely under their own control.

What does sovereignty actually mean in practice, beyond the buzzword?

It's not just "we host our own model." It spans infrastructure, security, governance, lifecycle management, hiring policy, supply chains, and vendor contracts. A genuinely sovereign AI stack means you're not dependent on a foreign cloud provider's terms of service, a foreign government's export policy, or a vendor's decision to deprecate an API you built critical workflows around.

Why this accelerated specifically in 2026:

- Enterprises watched AI model access get suspended and restored within weeks this year due to export control changes — a vivid, concrete demonstration of dependency risk that used to sound theoretical.
- Regulated industries face compliance requirements around data residency and model provenance that a third-party API simply can't satisfy, no matter how capable the model.
- The knock-on effects go well beyond IT: sovereignty decisions ripple into hiring (do you have the in-house talent to run this?), procurement, and long-term vendor relationships.

I've watched enterprises wrestle with a lighter version of this exact question for years around cloud versus on-premises infrastructure. Sovereign AI is that same debate, except the stakes now include which country's export policy might interrupt your production system with a week's notice.

Is your organization's AI dependency mapped, or just assumed to be stable?

Every time I think a trend has plateaued this year, another data point shows up a month later proving it hasn't. Worth staying humble about timelines.

-Ravi Kumar Gupta

Career gaps feel like an invisible scar on a résumé, turning every recruiter into a risk‑calculator and every hiring manager into a gatekeeper. I’ve seen this pattern repeat across industries: a few months off for health, family, or burnout suddenly becomes “too long,” and the candidate is labeled either overqualified for entry‑level roles or too risky for senior positions. The result is a vicious loop of underemployment, doubt, and endless job‑search fatigue.

The antidote is to stop treating the gap as a defect and start framing it as a strategic asset. First, rebuild the narrative with concrete outcomes rather than dates. A three‑month sabbatical spent caring for a relative can be presented as “managed a household budget of $X, optimizing resources and logistics under high‑stress conditions,” highlighting transferable skills like project management, problem‑solving, and resilience. Pair that story with a visible, up‑to‑date portfolio that demonstrates current technical competence-short, focused projects that solve real business problems, not just academic exercises. Even a single automation script that reduced a manual process by 30 % can speak louder than a list of past job titles.

Second, create a bridge role that aligns your existing expertise with emerging market demands. Instead of aiming directly for a traditional junior engineering position, target contract or consulting gigs that need a “hands‑on” technologist to integrate AI tools, improve DevOps pipelines, or modernize legacy systems. These roles are less risk‑averse because they are scoped, time‑boxed, and deliver immediate ROI. Success in a short‑term contract not only fills the résumé gap but also generates fresh references and measurable results you can showcase in the next application cycle.

Finally, treat education as a tool, not a rescue mission. If you’re considering a new degree, map each course to a specific competency gap that directly translates to a marketable skill. Enroll only in modules that culminate in a certifiable deliverable-such as a certified automation specialist badge-so the time and money spent become a tangible credential rather than an abstract credential.

By reshaping the gap into a story of purposeful growth, coupling it with demonstrable, up‑to‑date work, and strategically selecting bridge opportunities, you convert perceived risk into proven value. The market rewards evidence, not chronology.

【When AI Fails, the First Move Isn't the Fix】

When an AI system fails, the most expensive instinct isn't the fix. It's mis-sorting what kind of failure you're even looking at. A factory's defect-detection model misses a batch of cracked parts. They reach a customer and fail on the line. The engineer's first instinct is reasonable: quietly retrain, patch, move on. 

But the hard part of an AI incident usually isn't repair. It's classification — deciding which kind of incident this is, which law it lands in, which clock it starts, and who has to be the interface. Get the box wrong and every downstream step is late, or aimed at the wrong recipient. Three things practitioners routinely blur:

1. Failing ≠ high-risk. A quality-control vision model doesn't become an Annex III high-risk system just because it caused harm. Classification, conformity assessment, your role (provider vs deployer), and territorial scope decide that first. If it isn't high-risk, EU AI Act Article 73 incident reporting never triggers — the harm runs through existing machinery and product-safety vigilance and product liability instead.

2. Notify ≠ disclose. Article 73 reports to a market surveillance authority; GDPR Article 33 to a DPA; Article 34 to affected individuals; Article 86 gives a specific person an explanation. None of these is a press release to the public. And one event can start several parallel clocks at once — "waiting to see" is how you miss a statutory deadline.

3. Preserving evidence isn't defensive. It's how you later reconstruct root cause — and Article 73(6) can forbid altering the system in ways that compromise cause analysis before you notify. "Quietly patch the model" isn't just weak governance; it may breach the text.

The deeper discrimination is between two obligations people collapse into one. A product-safety incident — property, a business customer, a broken line — sits in product liability and contract. Article 86's right to explanation is a different container entirely: it applies when an Annex III system's output drives an individual decision about a natural person (hiring, credit, insurance, education) with legal or similarly significant effect. A machine misreading a part isn't that.

Precise incident response isn't courage under pressure. It's a script written in advance, where every step already names the role, the legal trigger, the deadline, the evidence, and who decides.
